system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2136-02-27 18:25:00 to 2136-02-28 16:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG and stents, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, diabetes, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted for chest pain that occurred one hour after a dialysis session. The pain was described as squeezing with back radiation and diaphoresis, similar to prior myocardial infarctions, but was unresponsive to sublingual nitroglycerin. Evaluation showed stable troponin levels and EKG changes without diagnostic evolution, indicating angina rather than acute myocardial infarction. The patient was managed with increased isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) to 120 mg daily, continued beta-blockade, and antiplatelet therapy. He remained chest pain-free, completed hemodialysis without complications, and was discharged home with cardiology follow-up and optimized anti-anginal regimen.

Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Ulcer of other part of foot

IMPRESSION:  Stable findings over multiple examinations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ . You came in today with chest pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. This morning I felt a little chest pressure, but it went away. I went to my dialysis like usual and felt fine after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then I went for a walk, and the pain came back—left side, sharp, and it spread to my lower back. I also felt nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you take your nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I wasn’t at home, so I didn’t have it with me. I walked to the ER instead. They gave me one there, and it helped right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s a good sign. Your EKG didn’t show any new changes, and we’ve checked your heart enzymes three times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re stable—no rise in troponin. That means no heart attack this time. It looks like your usual angina, triggered by activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not serious? But it felt just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important, but not an emergency. Your heart muscle wasn’t damaged. We’ll keep you overnight to monitor you and make sure it doesn’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I be worried about walking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can still be active, but listen to your body. If you feel chest pain, stop and rest. Use your nitroglycerin if it doesn’t go away in 5 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reviewed your meds. We’re increasing your amlodipine from 2.5 mg to 5 mg daily to help prevent these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my blood pressure? It runs low sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it. Your blood pressure today is 139 over 58, which is acceptable. Amlodipine helps relax your blood vessels and reduce the heart’s workload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve had a quiet night—no chest pain, and your vitals are stable. We’re planning to send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Should I change anything else besides the amlodipine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Keep taking all your other medications as before—especially your aspirin, metoprolol, and nitroglycerin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds in a day, call your doctor—it could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my dialysis—should I go as scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your regular dialysis. Your fistula looks good—no issues there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I’m very sensitive to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reduced your long-acting insulin from 12 to 6 units daily. That’s because you’re on dialysis, and your sugar can drop. Monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re going home with a diagnosis of stable angina—no new heart damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep your cardiology follow-up. If the chest pain changes—comes at rest, lasts longer, or doesn’t respond to nitro—go straight to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll watch for that and keep my pills straight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take it easy today, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate the care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with a history of coronary artery disease, prior CABG and stents, end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, diabetes, and peripheral vascular disease was admitted for chest pain that occurred after a dialysis session and walking. The pain was typical of his stable angina, associated with back pain and nausea, and resolved with sublingual nitroglycerin. Evaluation showed no EKG changes and stable cardiac enzymes, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. He was managed with observation, continuation of anti-anginal therapy, and an increase in amlodipine from 2.5 mg to 5 mg daily. His insulin glargine dose was reduced to 6 units daily due to dialysis-related sensitivity. He remained pain-free, was discharged home the next day with instructions to monitor weight and continue medications, and advised to follow up with cardiology.
